title: IETF Publishes RFC 10008, Adding the QUERY Method for Safe Requests With a Body
gist: The IETF published RFC 10008 in June 2026, adding QUERY as the first new standard HTTP verb since PATCH in 2010, giving developers a safe, idempotent, cacheable request method that can carry a body like POST — with early tooling support already landing in Rust, .NET, Axum, Quarkus and Bruno, though the author expects broad real-world adoption to take years.

insights.claim: The IETF published RFC 10008 in June 2026, adding QUERY as the first new standard HTTP verb since PATCH landed in 2010, authored by Julian Reschke, James Snell, and Mike Bishop, following a discussion Asbjørn Ulsberg reopened at the 2019 HTTP Workshop.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Marks a rare, notable event in HTTP protocol evolution (first new verb in 16 years) worth tracking for API/infrastructure implications.

themes.theme: Why QUERY exists: the GET/POST gap

insights.claim: QUERY exists to resolve a long-standing HTTP gap: GET is safe and idempotent but its filters must live in the URL, hitting length limits, leaking into access logs, and struggling to express nested structures, while POST can carry a rich body but is neither safe nor idempotent, so caches skip it and clients cannot safely retry it.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Explains the concrete technical motivation API designers should weigh when deciding whether to migrate search/filter endpoints from GET-with-query-params or POST-as-search hacks to QUERY.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'QUERY exists to settle an argument'

insights.claim: QUERY responses can remain cacheable as long as the cache key incorporates the request content, and servers can advertise QUERY support through the new Accept-Query HTTP header field.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A concrete mechanism (content-aware cache keys, Accept-Query) API and CDN teams need to implement correctly before they can safely rely on QUERY caching.
insights.locator: paragraph on cacheability and Accept-Query field

insights.claim: GraphQL and Elasticsearch already tunnel complex read queries through POST request bodies to work around GET's URL limitations, and QUERY offers a standards-based alternative that preserves cacheability for that same use case.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: API teams currently working around GET's limits with POST-based search endpoints (as GraphQL and Elasticsearch do) now have a standards path they can migrate toward once client, proxy, and cache support matures.

insights.claim: Even Cloudflare currently fakes a GET request to construct a cache key in order to cache POST responses, illustrating exactly the kind of workaround-hack that QUERY is meant to eliminate.
insights.speaker: Hacker News commenter, quoted by Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A concrete existing example of a major CDN provider hacking around the GET/POST caching gap, underscoring real market demand for a standard fix like QUERY.
insights.quote: Their unofficial support for caching POST requests is to create a fake GET request to serve as cache key and use that to cache the response. This is the kind of hacks everyone is forced to go through instead of using something like QUERY
insights.locator: Hacker News thread quote about Cloudflare

insights.claim: Early tooling support for QUERY has already merged into Rust's http crate and is being tracked across .NET, Axum, Quarkus, and Bruno, indicating framework-level adoption began within months of RFC publication.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A concrete adoption checklist — track whether a team's language/framework stack (Rust, .NET, Axum, Quarkus, Bruno) has QUERY support merged before committing to it in new API designs.
insights.locator: paragraph on GraphQL, Elasticsearch, and tooling support

insights.claim: The RFC explicitly frames QUERY as additive to GET and POST rather than a replacement, and the author notes that historical precedent from PATCH's adoption after 2010 suggests real-world QUERY adoption will likely be measured in years rather than months.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Sets realistic expectations for API teams: don't expect proxies, CDNs, and client libraries to universally support QUERY quickly — track proxy/cache/CDN support rollout as the real adoption indicator, not RFC publication itself.
insights.locator: paragraph on the specification advising additive treatment

themes.theme: Community debate: explicit method vs. GET-with-body

insights.claim: Community debate on r/webdev (800+ upvotes) largely rejected the idea of simply allowing an optional body on GET, arguing a distinct QUERY method makes support explicit — a server that doesn't support QUERY returns an explicit error, whereas a body silently dropped by an intermediary on GET is far harder to debug.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Explains the design rationale behind adding a new verb instead of extending GET semantics — relevant for anyone evaluating whether to push back on QUERY adoption in favor of a GET-with-body workaround.
insights.quote: Debugging why your request doesn't work is way easier. Because the server that does not support this method will say "QUERY not supported"
insights.locator: r/webdev thread discussion on optional GET body vs. QUERY

themes.theme: Why new HTTP methods are rare

insights.claim: New HTTP methods are rare in practice because each one must be reliably understood and supported across clients, servers, proxies, and caches before it becomes dependable, which is the structural reason both this idea and its practical adoption have taken years since first being raised in 2019.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A general principle for evaluating any future HTTP-level protocol change: adoption timelines should be measured against the full chain of client/server/proxy/cache support, not just standards-body publication.
insights.locator: closing paragraphs on HTTP working group (httpbis) and rarity of new methods
